Class WidgetHost<W extends net.minecraft.client.gui.components.events.GuiEventListener & net.minecraft.client.gui.components.Renderable>

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.AbstractPanelElement
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.WidgetHost<W>
Type Parameters:
W - the hosted widget's type
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
public class WidgetHost<W extends net.minecraft.client.gui.components.events.GuiEventListener & net.minecraft.client.gui.components.Renderable> extends AbstractPanelElement
Hosts a vanilla-style widget (anything that is a GuiEventListener and a Renderable) inside a panel, at the element's own rectangle. It is the one way MenuKit hosts a vanilla widget: TextField hosts vanilla's EditBox and Slider vanilla's slider through it, and a mod hosts a widget another library hands it (a config library's custom control) the same way. 
WidgetHost.builder()
        .widget(() -> library.makeWidget())
        .size(150, 20)
        .build();

What the host does every frame

  • Places it. A widget that is a vanilla LayoutElement is moved to the element's rectangle (setX, setY, and setWidth and setHeight on an AbstractWidget). Anything else is placed by the consumer's WidgetHost.Builder.place(WidgetHost.Placer) hook, which also wins over the LayoutElement path when given. The rectangle follows the panel, its scroll and any layout that moves the element.
  • Draws it, clipped to the element's rectangle (and, inside a ScrollContainer, to its viewport), with the mouse when the panel owns the pointer and none when another panel covers it or the host is disabled.

Input

The host routes the mouse itself, in screen coordinates, as an element: a click (with vanilla's double-click rule and the modifier keys held), the release of a press it took, the drag in between (followed every frame while the button is held) and the wheel. So the widget works wherever its panel is: on a standalone screen, on a panel over a vanilla screen, inside a scroll area or a tab. A click the widget takes gives it keyboard focus, as vanilla does.

Keys, typed characters, Tab and arrow-key focus moves and narration come from vanilla's focus: a stand-in for the widget is one of the screen's children (Focus), and forwards them to the widget while it holds focus. The stand-in is live only while the host is drawn and enabled, so a widget whose panel is hidden, whose tab is not shown or that is disabled is skipped by Tab and gives up focus on the next key, rather than typing unseen.

Overflow

A widget that opens a popup (a dropdown list) would be cut off at its rectangle. With WidgetHost.Builder.overflow(), while the widget holds keyboard focus it draws on top of the screen's panels, after the dialogs' layer and unclipped, and takes clicks anywhere on the screen: a click the widget does not take (outside it and its popup) ends its focus, which closes the popup. A host under a modal it does not belong to draws in place.

Inert, disabled, kinds

Like any element: under another panel's claim it gets no clicks and draws with no mouse; disabled (its own disabledWhen or its panel's) it takes no input and the stand-in is not focusable. The widget draws itself, so it looks the same on every kind of screen; an element built on the host (a TextField) chooses how its widget looks.

Lifecycle

The widget is made from the supplier on first need (the screen's init, in practice), not at build, since a vanilla widget may need the game's font.

    • isInteractive

      public boolean isInteractive()
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Whether this element handles pointer input, so a point on it is a solid claim on a transparent panel. Controls return true; render-only decorations keep the false default, so they never eat a click they do nothing with.
